subject: Career
title: The Communication Tax
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Communication Tax usable.

hook.text: The average worker spends 28% of their week on email and 20% searching for information. That's the communication tax.

buildup.text: Poor communication doesn't just waste time — it causes errors, missed deadlines, and conflict.

discovery.text: A Grammarly study found poor communication costs US businesses $1.2 trillion per year.

twist.text: The irony: we spend years learning technical skills but almost no time learning to communicate effectively.

climax.text: Clear communication is a force multiplier. One well-written message saves dozens of follow-ups.

punchline.text: Bad communication is the most expensive free thing in business.

quiz.question: How much does poor communication cost US businesses annually?

details.summary: The communication tax is the hidden cost of every additional person, channel, or meeting added to a project. As team size grows linearly, communication pathways grow exponentially, consuming an increasing share of productive time and creating coordination overhead.
details.whyItMatters: Brooks's Law states that adding people to a late project makes it later, largely due to communication tax. Understanding this dynamic helps leaders right-size teams and minimize overhead.
takeaways: Communication paths grow by the formula n times n minus one divided by two
Smaller teams often outperform larger ones in speed and quality
Reduce the tax by limiting channels, meetings, and approvals

faq.question: How do I calculate the communication tax for my team?
faq.answer: Count the unique communication pairs using the formula n(n-1)/2 where n is team size. A team of five has ten pairs; a team of ten has forty-five. Each pair represents a potential miscommunication, handoff, or meeting. Smaller sub-teams reduce this dramatically.

faq.question: What practical steps reduce communication tax without losing alignment?
faq.answer: Designate single points of contact between sub-teams, use documented decision logs instead of meetings, and limit cross-functional syncs to weekly cadences. Every recurring meeting should justify its existence against the cost it imposes.
